CULTURAL AFFAIRS-BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS. (B) LEVEL OF GOVERNMENT FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak today on a question of cut-backs in the field of arts and culture. One of the most disturbing aspects of these cut-backs that I have raised in a number of questions has been the surprise element, the betrayal, that the arts and cultural community has experienced.
The Conservatives while in Opposition, of course, said quite the contrary to what they are doing now. They were critical of the Liberal government for not being favourable enough and not giving enough support to arts and culture. During the election campaign the then Leader of the Opposition, now the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) replied to a letter sent to him on arts policy and spoke officially for the Party. This letter is dated August 21, 1984, addressed to Paul J. Reynolds of the Professional Association of Canadian Theatres. I want to read some of the promises which the Prime Minister, then Leader of the Opposition, made during the election campaign so we can look at the arts and culture cut-backs relative to the promises that were made. Part of this letter reads:
Our first order of business will be full consultation with the cultural sector on opportunities which should be pursued, and dangers which must be avoided. Opportunities, such as increased Canadian program production from live
February 11, 1985

performance companies, have not been promoted by current federal policy ... Our commitment to stimulate growth, ensure federal support through arm's length agencies and councils, and encourage alternative developments in film and program development are directed toward reversing the current low priority of cultural policy.
That is absolutely preposterous when we see what the Conservatives have done since they became the Government. Let me continue this litany of false promises:
We will seek better means to stimulate investment in the film, program and theatrical industries, and will ensure recognition of research and development costs, training and employment capacity ... We will ensure that federal cultural agencies have the mandate and resources to assist the cultural sector in taking new initiatives.
Instead, what we have had is cut-backs in existing funding for the Canada Council and in existing programming for the CBC. I continue:
We believe, for example, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation can play a stronger role in bringing Canadian performers, writers, designers, and companies both better employment opportunities and greater exposure.
Yes, the CBC could indeed be doing this, but it cannot if there are cut-backs. The CBC needs more funding. I agree the CBC needs a changed mandate and that there ought to be public input into that changed mandate. The CBC can hardly begin to do the kind of work in drama, entertainment, the kind of full programming that we want from it while it is experiencing these kinds of cut-backs.
Let me continue with the astonishing promises:
At the level of federal policy, however, there does not seem to be a sufficient understanding of the role of cultural growth to the social and economic future of Canada.
What did this Government proceed to do, Mr. Speaker? It has been quite ignorant of the economic contribution that the arts and culture industry has made. The letter continues:
In order to ensure that federal policy is better informed by the cultural sector, we will include in the Cultural Agencies legislation a guarantee that the Minister receives and responds to recommendations from the federal agencies which work most closely with the cultural sector. For the arm's length principle to have effect, advice to the Minister must be regular and accountable on both sides.
Yet the major arts agencies have not been able to get a meeting with the Minister, the groups who actually represent the artists who are doing the work in Canada. The major ones have not yet seen the Minister who manages to fly off to other countries, make speeches and spend a lot of taxpayers' money while he is preaching restraint here at home and has been absolutely unavailable to the community he is supposed to be serving.
I would like to point out the foolishness of these cut-backs in sheer economic terms. The arts industry makes an enormous contribution. It is the number 11 industry in Canada. It is about the same size as the electrical industry or the wood industry. More people are employed in arts than in manufacturing, and this is an industry that is growing.
Funding for the arts has enormous economic spin-offs. Let me give one example, Stratford. Stratford received a grant of $1.5 million. Its budget is $13 million, of which $8 million comes in through sales. It injects $35 million into the local economy. Stratford activities generated $9 million in provincial and federal tax revenues. In other words, Governments get
Adjournment Debate
back six times what they put in. Restaurants, motels and businesses in the tourist industry in the area receive an enormous amount from a very modest investment in terms of arts and culture expenditure.
To conclude, I want to stress the economic foolishness of the Government's cut-backs. This is what the arts and culture agencies and representative groups are stressing. I would like to see them argue the merits of the case in terms of the cultural contribution. Even on the Government's own stated criteria of helping the economy, these arts and culture cut-backs are foolishness indeed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the three-pronged question by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) has generated what looks like a 30 minute written response from our departmental officials. I will get as much as I can into my three minutes, and hope my Hon. friend will understand if I can not cover all the points she raised.
Let me state one important aspect of her "promises promises", speech. These budget reductions to the Canada Council, the National Film Board, the CBC or any other cultural agencies in no way diminish the importance which this Government attaches to the development of cultural expression in Canada. I can assure all Hon. Members of the personal commitment of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), of my own personal commitment, and indeed the strongly held view of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) to the maintenance of support which is essential to Canada's artists and this country's arts organizations as we come through this difficult economic period.
It is, however, the view of this Government that its most urgent priority is to arrest the growth of our national debt and to reverse the debilitating effect which debt service has on our ability to act on other national concerns. The burden of implementing such reductions must be shared by all, including the cultural sector. We are convinced, however, that the impact of these measures on individual artists and arts organizations can be greatly minimized through reductions in administrative expenditures, the elimination of non-essential services, of fat, if you will, plus greater involvement of the private sector.
The budget reductions to the Canada Council were $3.5 million and reductions to the National Arts Centre were $1 million. In the case of the Canada Council, this represents 4.8 per cent of the current parliamentary appropriation of approximately $72.5 million and 4.2 per cent of the Canada Council's total operating budget, which totals almost $84 million. The reduction to the National Arts Centre represents 6.2 per cent of its anticipated parliamentary appropriation of $16.16 million and 3.4 per cent of its total operating budget of $29.1 million.
The budgetary cut experienced by the National Film Board does not amount to twice as much as the ones made to other federal areas. They are equitably shared among the cultural

February 11, 1985
Adjournment Debate
agencies. Far from being unworthy of Government support, as it was suggested by the Hon. Member, the Government of Canada has given this cultural agency more importance by recently approving a new, more focused and more effective role by becoming a world-class centre of excellence in film and video production and a national training centre for advanced research, development and training in the art and technology of film and video.
With specific reference to the CBC cuts, of which we have been hearing so much lately, the Minister requested the CBC to make its budgetary reductions primarily in administrative areas and to protect programming as much as possible. The Minister made this request so that the reductions would affect as little as possible Canadian producers, artists and performers whose development the Government intends to encourage. The Minister cannot tell the CBC which programs to cut and which to leave in. That is the decision of the President of the CBC and its board of directors.

Worse, it has eliminated tourist projects from funding under federal programs.
I am quite aware that the Government has just signed a number of subsidiary agreements with several provinces-so much the better. But let us not be mistaken. First of all, these
agreements were going to be signed in any case, and second, they now represent the federal government's only contributions to the tourist industry.

subtopic: TOURISM-ELIMINATION OF FUNDING UNDER INDUSTRIAL AND REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM-CONSULTATION WITH INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to respond to questions put by the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud) on December 3 concerning the Government's decision to render tourism projects ineligible for grants under the Industrial and Regional Development Program.
[ Translation]
First of all, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his words of congratulations.

I want to assure Members of the House that the decision in no way changes the Government's view of the importance of tourism and its place in the over-all economy. In fact, it reflects our intention to reorient federal support for the tourism sector toward activities which would most benefit the national economy, while achieving better regional balance in our efforts.
February 11, 1985

As the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) stated in response to the relevant questions, we have determined that more effective and more regionally-sensitive tourism incentives can be delivered through tourism development sub-agreements with the various provinces and territories. In fact, we have agreements in place with Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan. The last six agreements were put in place by the new PC Government in the 20 weeks since it has been sworn in.
The total value of the six agreements, which I signed, is $229 million. Most of that money will come from the federal Treasury. Indeed, I have signed more tourism agreements, worth more money, and with more provinces, than did the previous Liberal Government in the entire period it was in office. By contrast, in the entire period in which the tourism sector was eligible for IRDP grants,the previous Government spent less than $30 million on tourism IRD projects.
In conclusion, I would indicate that discussions with officials in other provinces and Yukon have begun, and we anticipate having agreements in place with every province and territory before the end of the fiscal year. I also want to assure Members that the Government is prepared to use additional federal-provincial or federal-territorial agreements and special programs to meet the specific industry development requirements in the regions.
With respect to the Hon. Member's question concerning prior consultation with the industry, I have been in continual contact with the industry representatives, including the board of the Tourism Industry Association of Canada and the executive committee of the Canadian Restaurant and Foodservices Association, as well as with many other provincial bodies. In each case, the new tourism agreements have been explained and warmly received.
Given the amount of money which the federal Government is spending on tourism-many millions of dollars more than was spent by the previous Government-through sub-agreements in preference the IRDP arrangements, I am sure the Hon. Member will be eager to come into the House again to salute myself, the Prime Minister and the Government.
[ Translation]

subtopic: POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION A) YOUTH-BUDGETARY CUTS. (B) VALENTINE'S DAY CONFERENCE-REQUEST THAT STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES BE PERMITTED TO ATTEND
POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION A) YOUTH-BUDGETARY CUTS. (B) VALENTINE'S DAY CONFERENCE-REQUEST THAT STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES BE PERMITTED TO ATTEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity for debate with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mrs. Landry). At the time I held the position she holds now, and in my riding and elsewhere, people were wondering what a Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State does, whether it involved shorthand or what, and I am sure that now that she holds this position, the Hon. Member realizes that the Department of the Secretary of
Adjournment Debate
State is a fascinating one and that a lot of interesting things happen there.
I am glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary this evening, because on November 15 last year, I directed a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean) who gave me a very unsatisfactory answer, and I am sure that his Parliamentary Secretary, with her customary verve and wit, will do a far better job than the Minister.
Mr. Speaker, on November 15 I asked the Secretary of State: Will young people be represented at the National Economic Summit, the Valentine's Day Conference which is to be held in Regina? Will the voice of young Canada be heard? I know, Mr. Speaker, that you yourself want the voice of Canada's youth to be heard. At the time, the Secretary of State, spouting his usual generalities, said: Yes, yes, yes. Do not worry, consultation is the hallmark of our Government!
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State certainly did not act on what he said in the House, because when the time came to cut the Student Loans Program, among other things, he did not consult our students, he did not consult our young people. When the time came to announce the Flora '85 challenge, we all know that the real challenge to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) was to avoid youth representatives who wanted to talk about the Summer Canada program. We all know that.
The very day she held her press conference, students, the Canadian Federation of Students and young people across the country said: We were never consulted. During her press conference, the Minister of Employment and Immigration said: I consulted with large corporations and they promised me
10,000	jobs this summer. The Minister of Employment and Immigration must have let emotion or enthusiasm for her own program get the better of her, because today, in the press, business is reported as saying: We never said that.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that since its coming into power, this Government has done nothing to reach out to this multitude of lonely souls which make up our Canadian youth.
We know that the role of the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Champagne) has become incredibly insignificant. As I was saying recently, in her professional career, she always played major roles, but now she only plays two-bit parts. It is quite obvious since no issue has yet been addressed in important Fields such as employment or post-secondary education. The Minister of State for Youth has no mandate.
As a responsible or senior Minister, the Secretary of State should ensure that the Minister of State for Youth can play her role fully. There will soon be an important conference, a national summit, attended supposedly by nearly 120 participants. As we speak Mr. Speaker, no representative of a youth group has yet been invited. This truly shows contempt for 30 per cent of our people, and I am certain that if the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State has not realized it

February 11, 1985
Adjournment Debate
already, she will immediately act to correct this situation. I am convinced that, with her sensitivity, she realizes that it is completely unfair to leave 30 per cent of the people out of this new consultation process.
Consequently, in the coming discussions . .. We realize that the Secretary of State is preparing something in secret. We can see that he is planning something unpleasant with provincial representatives with regard to established programs financing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has announced that there will be cut-backs. Flowever, we know how much our post-secondary education system is underfinanced right now. It is not the right time to announce cutbacks, and if the Government is determined to do so, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no more fat to cut. As you are very familiar with the financial state of the University of Sherbrooke, you must know that it would be impossible to reduce expenditures more than has already been done. Consequently, if the Minister of Finance has ordered the Secretary of State to prepare cut-backs for the next Budget, it is essential that those directly involved, the major users of these services, be consulted.
It is unfortunate, but ever since this Government took office, a significant segment of the population has been completely ignored, and 1 think it is utterly disappointing. "Consultation" is the latest buzz word we hear in every speech. Before election day, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) kept talking about generosity. Now the key word is consultation, and it does not take much probing to find out that it is not real consultation.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) told me in this Flouse that she had had consultations on municipal job creation projects for youths with, among others, the mayor of Gander, when in fact she should have consulted the Canadian Federation of Municipalities. I would not know to what extent the municipality of Gander is representative of Canada as a whole, but my colleague from Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) called the mayor of his constituency and was told that no such program had ever been accepted.
Mr. Speaker, I am firmly convinced that, in the coming weeks and months, young Canadians will realize that this Government takes them for granted, ignores them altogether and makes them the victims of cutbacks, without consultations. I rest assured that the Parliamentary Secretary will be in a position to give us a definite answer as to whether young observers will be in Regina and whether young people will take an active part in the economic summit. That is what I expect from the Parliamentary Secretary, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure that, competent as she is, she will give us straight answers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to thank my hon. colleague from Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) for his kind words
with reference to me. I suggest that having held the portfolio of Secretary of State he has had good training, and I hope in a few years to be able to speak as eloquently as he does.
With respect to my concern about the problems faced by my Minister, the Secretary of State, it is my view that since he came to office he has already shown great interest and concern about the situation of the young, as regards more especially post-secondary education in Canada.
Concerning the reference to consultation, perhaps the Opposition Members should get their act together. At times they say that we consult too much, and at other times that we do not consult enough.
To answer more specifically the Hon. Member's question, 1 think that on November 15, the question was addressed specifically to the Secretary of State concerning his alleged lack of interest, especially on that day, concerning a student delegation visiting on Parliament Hill.
I would first like at this point to describe the circumstances surrounding that demonstration, to show the Minister's interest. The demonstration was held, like so many others throughout the Province, in relation with the work then being done by the Bovey Commission. The Ontario students had chosen November 15 because on that date the commissioners had intended to submit their report to the Ontario Minister of Colleges and Universities, the Hon. Bette Stephenson.
The students wanted to show that they were aware of the issues, that they were interested in a report that could have a considerable impact on them, and that they were concerned about the decisions that might come out of it. It was therefore strictly an Ontario demonstration.
However, 1 would like to add that the student organizations were greatly interested in the Canadian Government's role in the field of post-secondary education.
In that context, the Secretary of State met with the representatives of the Canadian Federation of Students hardly a week before the demonstration to discuss with them federal support for post-secondary education.
Mr. Speaker, 1 cannot overemphasize the importance given to that consultation by the government and the Secretary of State. All ministers have agreed to consult regularly with the groups under their jurisdiction. Since his appointment in mid-September, the Secretary of State has already met a good number of representatives from the main user groups of his Department. I refer among others to the Canadian Federation of Students, the Canadian Association of University Professors and the Canadian Association of Universities and Colleges.
Moreover, the Secretary of State has already met twice the Canadian Council of Ministers of Education and another meeting is scheduled for the near future in Ottawa, more specifically at the end of March. The purpose of those meetings is to discuss a few very important matters dealing with
February 11, 1985

assistance to education such as the financing of post-secondary education and the federal-provincial agreements on the use of official languages in education. In the opinion of Mr. McLean and his provincial colleagues, this is a useful dialogue, for it demonstrates the will of both levels of goverment to cooperate and consult, something which did not exist before.
Mr. Speaker, I have given these examples to show that the consultation process is definitely in motion. It should be
Adjournment Debate
emphasized that these exchanges of views are just starting, but that they will continue on a regular basis for the benefit of the Canadian people as a whole.
